meta.title: Rocket Builder: parts catalogue and assumptions

units.thrust: kN (per engine; sea level = ambient 101.325 kPa, vacuum = no ambient pressure)
units.isp: s (specific impulse; exhaust speed = Isp × g0, g0 = 9.80665 m/s²)

notes: Engine and booster figures come from the English Wikipedia article linked with each part (infobox values, read on the date above) unless another source is named.

A field listed in 'estimated' is not published or could not be confirmed for this edition: it was chosen from photographs, related engines or physical reasoning. Please check it before citing, and open an issue if you have a better source.

Where only one of the two thrusts is published, the other is derived at constant mass flow: F_vac = F_sl × Isp_vac / Isp_sl. For vacuum engines the sea-level thrust is F_vac − p0·A_exit, which is what a vacuum bell would give before the exhaust separates from the nozzle wall.

Between sea level and vacuum the builder interpolates honestly: the mass flow is fixed, so thrust falls linearly with ambient pressure, F(p) = F_vac − p·A_exit, with A_exit = (F_vac − F_sl)/p0. Specific impulse follows as F(p)/(ṁ·g0).

kerolox.name: Kerosene + oxygen
kerolox.why: Dense and easy to store: big thrust from compact tanks, so it is the classic first-stage propellant. The exhaust is sooty and orange.
kerolox.sigmaNote: Checked against the Saturn V first stage (S-IC: about 89 t of structure for 2,150 t of propellant, 4.1 %) and the Falcon 9 first stage (about 18 t for 411 t, 4.4 %).

hydrolox.name: Hydrogen + oxygen
hydrolox.why: The highest specific impulse of any common propellant, but hydrogen is 14 times less dense than water: huge, insulated, heavier tanks. The exhaust is nearly invisible.
hydrolox.sigmaNote: Between the Saturn V second stage (S-II: about 29 t of structure for 446 t, 6.5 %) and the third (S-IVB, about 11 % including its attitude-control modules); the lightweight Space Shuttle external tank managed 3.6 %.

methalox.name: Methane + oxygen
methalox.why: A middle road: better specific impulse than kerosene, burns clean (good for reuse), and can in principle be made on Mars from water and carbon dioxide.
methalox.sigmaNote: Estimate between kerosene and hydrogen stages; stainless-steel methane stages are heavy but simple.

tanks.usableNote: Only about 80 % of a tank section's cylinder volume holds usable propellant: the rest is domes, intertank or common bulkhead, thrust structure and ullage gas space. The Saturn V's stages manage about 0.7; Falcon 9's first stage, with chilled, densified propellant, nearly 1.0.
tanks.sizeNote: Small stages are relatively heavier (walls cannot be thinner than a practical minimum, and avionics and plumbing do not shrink): structure fraction = σ × (1 + 0.6 m / diameter). This reproduces the Electron (≈ 6 %), Falcon 9 (≈ 4.7 %) and Saturn V first stage (≈ 4.2 %) within about 10 %.
tanks.interstageNote: Interstage, separation system and adapters: 70 kg per m² of the upper stage's cross-section (Saturn V's S-IC/S-II interstage: 4.6 t for 79 m², about 58 kg/m²). Estimate.

engines.name: J-2
engines.flew: Saturn V second and third stages, Saturn IB upper stage

engines.name: RS-25
engines.flew: Space Shuttle main engines; Space Launch System core stage
engines.note: Thrust at 109 % of rated power level; throttles down to 67 % (0.61 of that).

engines.name: RL10B-2
engines.flew: Delta IV upper stage; SLS interim upper stage
engines.note: Vacuum engine with a carbon extendable nozzle.

engines.name: Merlin 1D
engines.flew: Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy first stages (sea-level version)

engines.name: Raptor 2
engines.flew: Starship Super Heavy booster and ship (sea-level version)
engines.note: Vacuum thrust derived at constant mass flow: 2,256 kN × 347 s / 327 s.

engines.name: Raptor Vacuum
engines.note: Figures for the version flown alongside Raptor 2 vary between sources; SpaceX has quoted about 380 s as a goal.

engines.name: RD-180
engines.flew: Atlas III and Atlas V first stage (two chambers, one set of turbopumps)

engines.name: BE-4
engines.flew: Vulcan Centaur first stage; New Glenn first stage
engines.note: Sea-level thrust 2,400 kN (550,000 lbf). Specific impulse has not been published; the values here are typical of methane staged-combustion engines.

engines.name: Vulcain 2.1
engines.note: Sea-level thrust derived at constant mass flow.

engines.name: Rutherford
engines.flew: Electron first stage (nine engines, 224 kN at liftoff)
engines.note: Sea-level thrust = the Electron's published 224.3 kN liftoff thrust ÷ 9. Battery-powered electric pumps.

boosters.name: Shuttle solid booster
boosters.fullName: Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster (four segments)
boosters.profileNote: Solid boosters cannot throttle: the grain is shaped so thrust dips through maximum dynamic pressure (max-q). This curve is a simplified shape of the published thrust trace; its peak gives ≈ 12.3 MN at liftoff (published: about 12.5 MN).

boosters.name: GEM 63
boosters.flew: Atlas V strap-on booster (up to five)

fairings.label: 5.2 m fairing
fairings.note: Falcon-class composite fairing: about 1.9 t for both halves (widely quoted; not in the infobox).

fairingJettisonNote: Fairings are dropped once aerodynamic heating is negligible, typically at 100–120 km.

payloads.name: 3U CubeSat
payloads.note: Three 10 cm cubes; the specification allows about 4 kg for a 3U (newer revisions allow up to 6 kg).

payloads.name: Small Earth-observation satellite
payloads.note: A small-launcher-class payload (the Electron's quoted capacity class, about 300 kg).

payloads.name: Geostationary communications satellite
payloads.note: A large geostationary satellite goes first to a geostationary transfer orbit (GTO); 6 t is typical of the heaviest (estimate).

payloads.name: Space telescope (JWST-class)
payloads.note: The James Webb Space Telescope launched folded, 6,161 kg, under a 5.4 m fairing, straight onto a path to the Sun–Earth L2 point.

payloads.name: Mars rover mission (Perseverance-class)
payloads.note: Cruise stage, aeroshell, descent stage and rover together.

payloads.name: Crew capsule (Dragon-class)
payloads.note: Capsule plus unpressurised trunk. The abort engines are built into the capsule, so there is no escape tower to drop.

payloads.name: Space-station module (Zarya-class)
payloads.note: The first module of the International Space Station (ISS), launched in 1998.

payloads.name: Apollo-class Moon ship
payloads.note: Command and service module (28,801 kg) + lunar module (15,103 kg) + adapter (≈ 1,800 kg), with a 4,170 kg launch escape tower that is dropped early in the second-stage burn.

payloads.name: Space station (Skylab-class)
payloads.note: Skylab, launched on the first two stages of a Saturn V in 1973.

payloads.name: Mass simulator
payloads.note: Dead weight you choose, as used on test flights.

leo.name: Low Earth orbit (LEO)
leo.note: About 7.8 km/s of orbital speed at 200 km, plus 1.5–2 km/s of gravity, drag and steering losses, minus up to 0.4 km/s from the Earth's rotation when launching east. 9.3–10 km/s is quoted; 9.4 km/s is a common round figure.

gto.name: Geostationary transfer orbit (GTO)
gto.note: A burn of about 2.44 km/s in LEO raises the far point to 35,786 km.

moon.name: Moon (trans-lunar injection)
moon.note: About 3.1–3.2 km/s in LEO puts a spacecraft on a path to the Moon (Apollo's trans-lunar injection).

l2.name: Sun–Earth L2
l2.note: Roughly the same energy as a trip to the Moon.

mars.name: Mars (trans-Mars injection)
mars.note: About 3.6 km/s from LEO in a good launch window (Hohmann-like transfer).

site.note: A generic coastal launch site at 28.5° N, launching due east: the Earth's rotation gives a free 408 m/s.
